title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count things and people, ask 'how many / how much', give your age and use ordinals (first to tenth).
intro:
Learn the numbers 0–100 from the **Numbers** chart in this course — Malayalam numbers are fairly regular after 20: tens + -ത്തി- + unit (ഇരുപത്തിയൊന്ന് 21, മുപ്പത്തിരണ്ട് 32). Large amounts are counted in **lakhs** (ലക്ഷം, 100,000) and **crores** (കോടി, 10 million), not millions.

This unit is about *using* numbers: how many, how much, how old, and which one in order.

vocab.note: ഒന്ന് is the counting form; ഒരു goes before nouns: ഒരു ചായ 'a/one tea'.
അര കിലോ 'half a kilo'; quarter is കാൽ (kāl): കാൽ കിലോ.
Comes after the word: ഒന്ന് മാത്രം 'only one'.

phrases.en: How old are you? (lit. how many years have become to you?)
What's your phone number? (lit. how much is…)
This is my first trip to Kerala.
I don't need both, one is enough.

grammar.title: Numbers with nouns
grammar.body:
The number comes **before** the noun. 'One' has a special attributive form **ഒരു** *oru* (ഒരു ചായ 'one tea'); the others are often said with a final -u before a noun: രണ്ടു, മൂന്നു, നാലു (written either രണ്ട് or രണ്ടു).

After a number, people-nouns usually take the plural (മൂന്ന് കുട്ടികൾ 'three children'), but things often stay singular in everyday speech (രണ്ട് ചായ 'two teas').

To count people, use **പേർ** *pēr* ('persons'): രണ്ടു പേർ 'two people', എത്ര പേർ? 'how many people?'. Adding **-ഉം** to a number means 'all of them': രണ്ടും 'both', മൂന്നും 'all three'.

grammar.title: How many, how old, which one
grammar.body:
**എത്ര** *etra* asks 'how many / how much'. It also asks for numbers in general (phone number, time, price).

**Age** is expressed as years that have 'become' (ആയി *āyi*, 'became') to someone, with the dative: എനിക്ക് മുപ്പത് **വയസ്സായി** 'I'm thirty'. For children you'll also hear അവന് അഞ്ചു വയസ്സുണ്ട് 'he has five years'.

**Ordinals**: add **-ആമത്തെ** (-āmatte) to the number: രണ്ടാമത്തെ 'second', പത്താമത്തെ 'tenth'. ആദ്യത്തെ *ādyatte* 'first' and അവസാനത്തെ *avasānatte* 'last' are very common. Shorter -ആം forms appear in fixed expressions: ഒന്നാം ക്ലാസ് 'first standard (grade 1)'.

dialogue.title: Grandma meets a new neighbour's child
dialogue.setting: Ammooma (grandmother) talks to Anu, a little girl, on the veranda.

lines.speaker: Ammooma
lines.en: What's your name, dear? (lit. daughter's name?)

lines.speaker: Anu
lines.native: എനിക്ക് എട്ട് വയസ്സായി. ഞാൻ മൂന്നാം ക്ലാസ്സിലാ.
lines.roman: enikkŭ eṭṭŭ vayassāyi. ñān mūnnām klāssilā.
lines.en: I'm eight. I'm in third standard.

lines.speaker: Ammooma
lines.en: How many people are at home?

lines.speaker: Anu
lines.native: അഞ്ചു പേർ. അച്ഛൻ, അമ്മ, രണ്ട് ചേട്ടന്മാർ, പിന്നെ ഞാൻ.
lines.roman: añju pēr. acchan, amma, raṇḍŭ chēṭṭanmār, pinne ñān.
lines.en: Five. Dad, Mum, two big brothers, and me.

lines.speaker: Ammooma
lines.en: Oh! How old are your brothers?

lines.speaker: Anu
lines.en: One is twelve, the other is fifteen.

culture: Indian number grouping is used in Kerala: 1,00,000 is one lakh and 1,00,00,000 is one crore, and prices, salaries and populations are always quoted this way. Adults are often affectionately called മോൻ / മോൾ (son / daughter) by older people — Ammooma's മോളുടെ പേരെന്താ? is completely natural even to a stranger's child.
